title: Justice’s Long Ascent - Supreme Court Observer
summary: The Order of suspension of sentence for two convicts in the Bilkis Bano’s matter acts against its own institutional memory On 28 October, the Division Bench of Justice M.M. Sundresh and P.B. Varale suspended the sentences of two convicts—Bipinchandra Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya—who were convicted in the Bilkis Bano gangrape case and the.

note.Facts: The Division Bench of Justice M.M. Sundresh and P.B. Varale suspended the sentences of two convicts (Bipinchandra Joshi and Pradip Modhiya) in the Bilkis Bano gang-rape and murder case, citing long incarceration and Joshi’s disability, and questioning the conviction on the basis that one convict was not named in the original FIR.
note.Issue: Whether a life sentence may be suspended on the grounds raised by the appellants, particularly the reliance on the original FIR and the alleged disability of a convict, given the gravity of the offences.
note.Held: The order suspended the sentences, accepting the appellants’ contentions despite objections from the Additional Solicitor General and without detailed reasoning.
note.Principle: Suspension of a life sentence must be granted only in exceptional circumstances, with due regard to the seriousness of the offence; reliance solely on the original FIR to set aside a conviction is not permissible where the trial courts have already affirmed the conviction on survivor testimony.
note.Provisions: Section 435 CrPC (remission), Section 389 CrPC (cancellation of suspension of sentence), *Rajesh Upadhyay v. State of Bihar* (2025), *Preet Pal Singh v. State of U.P.* (2020).
note.Exam angle: CrPC – discuss the criteria for suspension/remission of life sentences under §§ 389 and 435, and how Supreme Court precedents (*Rajesh Upadhyay*, *Preet Pal Singh*) frame the limits of such orders.

title: Supreme Court To Examine Whether Former Mutawalli Can Represent Waqf As Sajjadanashin After Tenure Ends
summary: The dispute arose after the Waqf Tribunal dismissed the Dargah's suit seeking a declaration that certain properties were Waqf properties, on the ground that the person representing it no longer held the position of Mutawalli.

note.Facts: A former Mutawalli of a Dargah continued to represent the Waqf in a suit after his tenure expired, claiming he was also a Sajjadanashin, an office without a fixed term.
note.Issue: Whether, in the absence of a Waqfnama, Waqf deed or pleaded custom establishing him as Sajjadanashin, a former Mutawalli can represent the Waqf after his Mutawalli tenure ends.
note.Held: The Supreme Court has not yet decided; it has listed the matter for further hearing to examine the question.
note.Principle: The Court must determine if representation can persist without documentary proof (Waqfnama or deed) or pleaded custom of Sajjadanashin status once the Mutawalli’s term has expired.
note.Exam angle: Waqf Act – issue of who may represent a Waqf institution in litigation; could be asked on the requirement of a Waqfnama or custom to establish Sajjadanashin status versus tenure-based authority of a Mutawalli.

title: Delhi High Court Declines Death Penalty For Cop Convicted Of Double Murder, Says Breach Of Public Trust Alone Can't Justify Capital Punishment
case_name: Vimpy Chaddha v. State of NCT of Delhi & Anr
summary: The Delhi High Court has upheld the life sentence awarded to a police officer convicted of murdering two persons in 2011, observing that his abuse of the position of trust reposed in him as a protector of citizens constituted a significant aggravating circumstance.

note.Facts: Police officer Ajay Kumar Tomar, in uniform, robbed and shot Amarjeet Singh Chadha on 24 Sept 2011 and, while fleeing, shot civilian motorcyclist Harender Singh (alias Sunny), who later died.
note.Issue: Whether the officer’s breach of public trust and the gravity of the murders justify enhancement of the life sentences to the death penalty.
note.Held: The Delhi High Court upheld the trial court’s life sentences and rejected the pleas for capital punishment.
note.Principle: Abuse of a position of public trust is an aggravating factor, but alone cannot constitute a ground for death-penalty; capital punishment requires evidence of exceptional brutality, depravity or irredeemability.
note.Exam angle: Could be asked under the IPC’s provisions on murder and death-penalty sentencing, focusing on the test for aggravation versus the requirement of “exceptional” circumstances for capital punishment.

title: Daughter-In-Law Can't Be Expected To Vacate Senior Citizen's House Without Assured Alternate Accommodation: Delhi High Court
case_name: Namrata Yadav v. Ramesh Kumar Yadav & Ors
ratio: A daughter-in-law cannot be expected to vacate her senior citizen in-laws' house and relocate to an alternate accommodation without certainty regarding its standard…
summary: The Court was hearing a petition filed by a woman challenging an order passed under the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, directing her and her son to vacate the property occupied by them.

note.Facts: A daughter-in-law and her son were ordered to vacate the senior-citizen in-laws’ house under the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, after the in-laws alleged harassment; the daughter-in-law claimed the house was her matrimonial home under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005.
note.Issue: Whether a daughter-in-law can be compelled to vacate the senior-citizen’s house without a guaranteed, suitably standardised alternate accommodation.
note.Held: The Delhi High Court upheld the eviction order in principle but modified it, directing the in-laws to provide specific alternate accommodation (rent up to ₹35,000 and six months’ advance) and allowing the daughter-in-law four weeks to identify suitable housing, thereby protecting her right to residence.
note.Principle: A daughter-in-law’s right to reside in a shared household is not absolute; eviction must be accompanied by assured, adequate alternate accommodation to avoid rendering the residential right illusory.
note.Provisions: Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007; Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005; no specific sections or cases cited in the source.
note.Exam angle: Questions may test the interplay of the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 with the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, focusing on the balance of senior citizens’ right to peaceful living against a daughter-in-law’s right to residence and the requirement of guaranteed alternate accommodation.

title: Senior Citizen Can't Be Compelled To Share Own House With Children Against Wishes: Delhi High Court
summary: The Court set aside orders passed by the District Magistrate and the Divisional Commissioner rejecting his eviction plea under the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, and directed the son and daughter-in-law to vacate the property within four weeks.

note.Facts: An 85-year-old owner of a self-acquired house in Delhi filed a petition for eviction of his eldest son and daughter-in-law, alleging harassment, threats and assault, and seeking relief under the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007.
note.Issue: Whether a senior citizen can be compelled to share his own house with his children against his wishes when he alleges harassment, and what evidentiary standard is required under the Senior Citizens Act for eviction.
note.Held: The Delhi High Court set aside the orders of the District Magistrate and Divisional Commissioner and directed the son and daughter-in-law to vacate the property within four weeks, holding that the senior citizen’s right to peaceful, dignified residence outweighs the requirement of proving harassment by the stringent civil standard.
note.Principle: Under the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, a senior citizen may obtain eviction of children from his own property if he demonstrates that the property needs protection for him to live peacefully and with dignity; the Act does not impose a requirement of “clear and cogent” evidence of harassment, and summary proceedings may rely on the overall factual matrix, including police complaints.
note.Provisions: Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007; Delhi Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Rules, 2009; *Ravi Kant Gupta v. State of Uttar Pradesh*; *Pritam Singh v. Government of NCT of Delhi*.
note.Exam angle: Questions may test the application of the Senior Citizens Act – e.g., “Discuss the criteria for eviction of children from a senior citizen’s property under the Act and the evidentiary standards required,” or “Analyse how the High Court’s interpretation of ‘protection of property’ expands the scope of relief under the Act.”

title: Fresh Divorce Petition Maintainable Despite Earlier Withdrawal Without Liberty To Refile On Jurisdictional Grounds: Delhi High Court
ratio: Procedural provisions cannot be applied in a manner that defeats substantive matrimonial rights…
summary: The Delhi High Court has held that withdrawal of a divorce petition due to a defect in territorial jurisdiction, even without obtaining liberty to institute a fresh petition.

note.Facts: The husband withdrew a 2021 divorce petition filed in Gurugram Family Court for lack of territorial jurisdiction without seeking liberty to re-file, and later instituted a fresh petition in Dwarka Family Court; the wife sought dismissal of the second petition under Order XXIII Rule 1(4) CPC.
note.Issue: Whether a divorce petition withdrawn for a jurisdictional defect, without liberty to institute a fresh suit, bars the filing of a subsequent petition on the same matrimonial claim.
note.Held: The Delhi High Court allowed the fresh petition, holding that the earlier withdrawal does not bar a new suit where the withdrawal was made bona-fide due to lack of jurisdiction and not to abandon the claim.
note.Principle: A withdrawal of a matrimonial suit for a jurisdictional defect, without intent to abandon the claim, does not invoke Order XXIII Rule 1(4) CPC to bar a fresh petition; procedural rules cannot defeat substantive matrimonial rights unless the statute expressly mandates such consequence.
note.Provisions: Order VII Rule 11 CPC; Order XXIII Rule 1(4) CPC; *Nidhi Jain v. Ankit Jain* (distinguished).

title: Child's Welfare Paramount In Custody Disputes, Not Parents' 'Battle Of Wits And Egos': Delhi High Court
summary: Justice Neena Bansal Krishna made the observation while disposing of a contempt petition filed by a father alleging that his estranged wife was deliberately disobeying a Family Court order granting him visitation rights to meet their minor son.

note.Facts: A father filed a contempt petition alleging his estranged wife deliberately violated a Family Court order granting him visitation rights to their minor son; the parties had a settlement permitting visitation, but the mother allegedly obstructed it and has an appeal pending.
note.Issue: Whether the mother’s alleged non-compliance with the visitation order amounts to contempt, or whether the matter should be decided by the Family Court on execution/modification of the order.
note.Held: The Delhi High Court declined to entertain contempt proceedings, directing the Family Court to consider the father’s execution petition and pass appropriate orders.
note.Principle: In custody and visitation disputes, the child’s welfare is paramount and alleged breaches of visitation orders must be resolved by the competent Family Court, not through contempt proceedings at the interim stage.
note.Exam angle: Application of the Family Courts Act (guardianship and visitation orders) – could be asked on the test as an issue-framing question about the proper forum and the primacy of the child’s best interests in custody disputes.
